```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
gc <- read_csv(file.path(res, "genes_by_community.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
go <- read_csv(file.path(res, "genes_by_outcome.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sp <- read_csv(file.path(res, "species_by_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cs <- read_csv(file.path(res, "contrast_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
grp <- read_csv(file.path(res, "sample_groups.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
tg <- read_csv(file.path(res, "top_gene_counts.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
n_sig <- function(x) sum(x$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
n_big <- function(x) sum(x$padj < 0.05 & abs(x$log2FoldChange) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)

# toy example for size factors: sample C was sequenced twice as deeply
toy_depth <- c(A = 1, B = 1, C = 2)
toy_sf <- toy_depth / exp(mean(log(toy_depth)))   # geometric mean of 1, as DESeq2 scales them
toy_raw <- c(A = 50, B = 48, C = 100)

# both gene contrasts in one table, for the side-by-side volcano
vol <- bind_rows(community = gc, outcome = go, .id = "contrast") |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(call = case_when(padj >= 0.05 ~ "not significant",
                          abs(log2FoldChange) > 1 ~ "significant, more than 2-fold",
                          TRUE ~ "significant, less than 2-fold"),
         contrast = fct_inorder(recode(contrast,
           community = paste0("genes ~ community: ", scales::comma(n_sig(gc)),
                              " significant, ", n_big(gc), " more than 2-fold"),
           outcome = paste0("genes ~ birth outcome: ", scales::comma(n_sig(go)),
                            " significant, ", n_big(go), " more than 2-fold"))))
```

## This morning you built a column {.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
grp |> filter(time_point == "week_18") |> count(community) |> kable()
```

These are the week 18 samples only, one per person.

. . .

You built `community` from the **species** table. Now we test the **gene**
table with it.

## The question {.center}

For each feature, is its count systematically different between two groups of
samples?

. . .

In the gene table we ask it about 14,000 times, once per gene.

## Counts break the assumptions of a t-test

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Counts can't go below zero, and they are skewed.
- The variance depends on the mean: a gene at 10 counts behaves differently
  from one at 10,000.
- Library sizes differ, so raw counts aren't comparable between samples.
- Estimating each gene's variance on its own, from 157 samples, ignores what
  the other 14,000 genes can tell you.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6.5
tg |>
  filter(symbol == "SERPINB12") |>
  ggplot(aes(normalised_count)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = pal[["navy"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "SERPINB12 in 157 week 18 samples",
       x = "normalised count", y = "number of samples")
```
:::
::::

## The variance really does track the mean

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.8
gc |>
  filter(!is.na(lfcSE), baseMean > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(baseMean, lfcSE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.8, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_smooth(colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.3, se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "mean count across samples (log scale)",
       y = "uncertainty in the fold change (log scale)")
```

Fold changes for low-count genes are much less certain. A method built for
counts uses this trend to borrow information across genes.

## Running DESeq2

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = gene_counts,          # features x samples, raw counts
  colData   = sample_table,         # one row per sample, same order
  design    = ~ community
)

dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("community", "anaerobe", "lactobacillus"))
```

. . .

Give it raw counts, never CPM and never logged values. DESeq2 does its own
normalisation, and feeding it normalised data breaks it.

## Inside `DESeq()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. **Size factors.** Works out how deeply each sample was sequenced, so samples
   become comparable.
2. **Dispersion.** Estimates each feature's variance, then pulls extreme
   estimates toward the trend you just saw.
3. **Test.** Fits a model per feature and tests whether the group term is zero.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
A toy gene in three samples. Sample C was sequenced twice as deeply.

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(sample = names(toy_raw), raw = toy_raw,
       `size factor` = round(toy_sf, 2),
       normalised = round(toy_raw / toy_sf)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

Dividing by the size factor puts the three samples back on one scale.
:::
:::
::::

## The results table

```{r}
#| echo: false
gc |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(gene = symbol, baseMean = round(baseMean), log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            stat = round(stat, 1), pvalue = format(pvalue, digits = 2), padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  head(5) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- `log2FoldChange` of 1 means twice as much, and -1 means half as much.
- `pvalue` is per feature, before any correction.
- `padj` is what you report.
:::

## Testing 13,738 genes at once

If no gene differed at all, how many would have `pvalue` below 0.05?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.8
n_null <- sum(!is.na(gc$pvalue)) * 0.05
gc |>
  filter(!is.na(pvalue)) |>
  ggplot(aes(pvalue)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), fill = pal[["navy"]], colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n_null, linetype = 2, colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.98, y = n_null, vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1, colour = pal[["orange"]],
           label = "expected per bar if no gene differed", size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "pvalue (bars 0.05 wide)", y = "number of genes")
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
About **687**, one in every twenty genes. The spike in the first bar is the real
signal sitting on top of that.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
That is why `padj` exists. Benjamini-Hochberg controls a different error: of
the features you call significant, roughly 5% are wrong.
:::
:::
::::

## Volcano plot: anaerobe against Lactobacillus

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5.6
gc |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(call = case_when(padj >= 0.05 ~ "not significant",
                          log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "up in anaerobe",
                          TRUE ~ "up in Lactobacillus")) |>
  ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = call)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("not significant" = pal[["grey"]],
                                 "up in anaerobe" = pal[["orange"]],
                                 "up in Lactobacillus" = pal[["teal"]])) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10 adjusted p", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## `r scales::comma(n_sig(gc))` significant genes, led by the epithelial barrier {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
gc |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(gene = symbol, name = str_trunc(gene_name, 46),
            log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2)) |>
  head(10) |> kable(align = "llr")
```

Mucins, filaggrin and cornified envelope proteins are epithelial barrier genes,
and all of these are higher where Lactobacillus dominates. We did not put that
pattern there; it came with the real samples.

## Always plot the top hit

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 4.8
tg |>
  mutate(lab = paste0(symbol, "  (log2FC ", round(log2FoldChange, 2), ")")) |>
  ggplot(aes(community, normalised_count, fill = community)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.75, width = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]])) +
  facet_wrap(~lab, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "normalised count (log scale)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Every fold change here is negative, and every boxplot is higher on the
Lactobacillus side, so the picture and the sign agree.

## Check the direction every time {.center}

Getting the direction of a contrast backwards is the most common error in this
analysis. Nothing warns you and the table looks normal, so it regularly
survives peer review.

. . .

A boxplot of the top gene, like the one on the last slide, shows the direction
at a glance.

## Significant is not the same as large

```{r}
#| echo: false
cs |>
  mutate(contrast = factor(contrast, levels = c("genes_by_community", "genes_by_outcome",
                                                "genes_by_bv", "species_by_outcome"))) |>
  arrange(contrast) |>
  mutate(contrast = recode(contrast,
    genes_by_community = "genes ~ community (from the 16S table)",
    genes_by_outcome   = "genes ~ birth outcome",
    genes_by_bv        = "genes ~ Nugent-defined BV",
    species_by_outcome = "species ~ birth outcome")) |>
  transmute(contrast, `features tested` = scales::comma(features_in),
            samples, `padj < 0.05` = scales::comma(n_sig),
            `and |log2FC| > 1` = scales::comma(n_sig_lfc1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

. . .

Compare the first two rows: a similar number of significant genes, and a very
different number of large changes.

## Similar numbers of hits, different kinds of hit

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(vol, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = call)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~contrast) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("not significant" = pal[["grey"]],
                                 "significant, less than 2-fold" = pal[["navy"]],
                                 "significant, more than 2-fold" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10 adjusted p", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

Community moves a few hundred genes a long way. Birth outcome moves a great many
genes a little.

. . .

Friday we come back to this: thousands of significant genes, and still a poor
prediction of who delivers early.

## A warning about proxies

```{r}
#| echo: false
cs |> filter(contrast %in% c("genes_by_community", "genes_by_bv")) |>
  mutate(grouping = recode(contrast,
    genes_by_community = "Lactobacillus fraction, computed from the 16S table",
    genes_by_bv = "Nugent score of 7 or more, read down a microscope")) |>
  transmute(grouping, samples, `genes at padj < 0.05` = scales::comma(n_sig)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

. . .

Both groupings ask whether the community is disturbed. The one built from data
you already have finds hundreds of times as many genes.

## Other people's tools

We used DESeq2 on both tables, because the point this week is that both tables
are count tables. Not everyone does that.

| for gene counts | for microbial counts |
|---|---|
| DESeq2, edgeR | ALDEx2, ANCOM-BC |
| limma-voom | MaAsLin 2, corncob |
| | DESeq2, still, often |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

. . .

The microbiome tools exist because that table is compositional and sparse in a
way gene tables are not. The case for them is worth reading before you publish a
microbiome analysis.

## Don't test the species table with `community` {.center}

You built `community` from the species table, so testing the **gene** table
with it is fine.

. . .

Testing the **species** table with it is circular. You would be asking whether
samples with lots of Lactobacillus have lots of Lactobacillus.

## The exercise tests species against birth outcome

```{r}
#| eval: false
# the grouping comes from the clinic, not from either count table
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(species_counts, sample_table, ~ outcome)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
sp |> filter(!is.na(padj), padj < 0.05) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(species = str_replace_all(species, "_", " "),
            log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  head(5) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```

`r n_sig(sp)` of `r cs$features_in[cs$contrast == "species_by_outcome"]` species
are significant, and `r sum(sp$padj < 0.05 & sp$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)`
of them are higher in the people who delivered early.
